extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century readers of The Spectator; readers interested in manners, marriage, fashion, and moral/social observation
extracted.subtask_description: Short, moralizing periodical essays on manners, marriage, and society (Spectator-style) mixing social observation, wit, and practical counsel for a general educated public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for Board of the Fashionable Society
rubrics_metrics.description: Old Beaus are to be presented in the first place; but as that Sect, with relation to Dress, is almost extinct, it will... be absolutely necessary to take in all Time-Servers, properly so deem'd; that is, such as, without any Conviction of Conscience or View of Interest, change with the World, and that merely from a Terror of being out of Fashion. Such also, who from Facility of Temper, and too much Obsequiousness, are vicious against their Will, and follow Leaders whom they do not approve, for Want of Courage to go their own Way, are capable Persons for this Superintendency. Those who are both to grow old, or would do any thing contrary to the Course and Order of things, out of Fondness to be in Fashion, are proper Candidates. To conclude, those who are in Fashion without apparent Merit, must be supposed to have latent Qualities, which would appear in a Post of Direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrounding guidance: lists to be sent in within fourteen days; chief coffee-houses to nominate two or three among themselves; the physician post is already engaged. The proposal treats fashion-direction as an office for people who habitually shift with trends, are obsequious or follow leaders, or who lack obvious merit but may reveal latent qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid theatrical and romantick styles in courting and marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: We generally make Love in a Style, and with Sentiments very unfit for ordinary Life: They are half Theatrical, half Romantick. By this Means we raise our Imaginations to what is not to be expected in human Life; and because we did not beforehand think of the Creature we were enamour'd of as subject to Dishumour, Age, Sickness, Impatience or Sullenness, but altogether considered her as the Object of Joy, human Nature it self is often imputed to her as her particular Imperfection or Defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: do not build courtship on inflated, theatrical expectations; anticipate human flaws (age, illness, temper) so that ordinary life does not become a source of perpetual disappointment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve a disposition to be pleased
rubrics_metrics.description: I take it to be a Rule proper to be observed in all Occurrences of Life, but more especially in the domestick or matrimonial Part of it, to preserve always a Disposition to be pleased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: This disposition is maintained by considering things in their right light, as Nature has form'd them, and not as our own Fancies or Appetites would have them. It counsels tempering desire with just appraisal of circumstances to sustain contentment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let reason support passion; adapt yourself to the circumstances of married life
rubrics_metrics.description: But the Man who brings his Reason to support his Passion, and beholds what he loves as liable to all the Calamities of human Life... will form himself accordingly, and adapt his Mind to the Nature of his Circumstances. This latter Person will be prepared to be a Father, a Friend, an Advocate, a Steward for People yet unborn...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: readiness for the duties of marriage—patience with children/noise, accepting new cares and relations—comes from subordinating ungoverned passion to reason and realistic expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincere affection grounded in duty, honour, and friendship produces domestic happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Affection is well-placed, and supported by the Considerations of Duty, Honour, and Friendship, which are in the highest Degree engaged in this Alliance, there can nothing rise in the common Course of Life... in which a Man will not find Matters of some Delight unknown to a single Condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects described: sincere, duty-infused love allows one to find pleasure in indifferent things, doubles satisfactions because others participate, and mitigates afflictions since others share burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: When married to a spirited or difficult partner practise patience and use correction sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: When these (perverse Jades) are joined to Men of warm Spirits, without Temper or Learning, they are frequently corrected with Stripes; but one of our famous Lawyers is of Opinion, That this ought to be used sparingly... I should rather recommend to those who are visited with Women of Spirit, to form themselves for the World by Patience at home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and example: invoke Socrates' reported forbearance (Xantippe anecdotes) as virtue—endure and learn from domestic trials; correction (physical) is not endorsed as a first or frequent remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept honours or favours without merit; distinctions are only useful insofar as they enable public action
rubrics_metrics.description: I humbly conceive, that all Distinctions are useful to Men, only as they are to act in Publick; and it would be a romantick Madness, for a Man to be a Lord in his Closet... Those who accept of Favour without Merit, support themselves in it at the Expence of your Majesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: prefer the interior consciousness of well-doing to outward titles; the writer praises modest refusal of honours when they would only produce public observation without corresponding ability; warns that patronage without merit is wasteful of sovereign resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid construing others' misfortunes as divine punishment; religion should incline to goodwill
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot be guilty of a greater Act of Uncharitableness, than to interpret the Afflictions which befal our Neighbours, as Punishments and Judgments... This Humour of turning every Misfortune into a Judgment, proceeds from wrong Notions of Religion, which, in its own nature, produces Goodwill towards Men...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: such constructions aggravate suffering and reduce compassion; moral guidance is to put the mildest construction on accidents and to recognize that a gloomy temper, not true religion, produces spiteful interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate delight in small domestic observations as evidence of affectionate character
rubrics_metrics.description: He who sincerely loves his Wife and Family, and studies to improve that Affection in himself, conceives Pleasure from the most indifferent things... (anecdote: a father delighted by an infant's remark about the clock as a sign of prescience)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: valuing small domestic occurrences—children's sayings, petty family anecdotes—is a sign of affectionate engagement and contributes to household happiness; being easily pleased yields social and personal rewards.
